                               G-9 AND G-13 LANDOWNERS’
                          EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

        G-9 and G-13 Landowners timely files these Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (PFD)

for consideration by the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) and respectfully shows

as follows:

                                        I.     INTRODUCTION

        The G-9 and G-13 Landowners are made up of three landowners1 who would be directly

affected by any decision the Commission makes in this proceeding. The extensive participation

by landowners speaks to how impactful the proposed transmission line would be to the community

and to the State.2 As such, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners appreciate the thorough analysis by the

administrative law judges (ALJs) in the Proposal for Decision (PFD).




         1
           The G-9 and G-13 Landowners include Jeff Kubin acting in the interest of The Highgate West Group LLC
(d/b/a The Highgate Group LLC) (owners of tract 2141), Bub Guthrie acting in the interest of Guthrie Ranching LTD
(owners of tracts 2127 and 2128), and James Giddens acting in the interest of JKME Family Limited Partnership
(owners of tracts 2147 and 5142).
        2
            SOAH Proposal for Decision with Memorandum at 12 (Aug. 20, 2026) (Proposal for Decision).

                                                       2
        Specifically, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners support the ALJs’ recommendation that the

two transmission lines that make up Import Path 2, Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-

Sand Lake, should not be approved.3 The ALJs appropriately found that Oncor Electric Delivery

Company LLC and LCRA TSC (collectively, Applicants) failed to establish that Import Path 2 is

necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.4 As set forth in

the G-9 and G-13 Landowners witnesses Jeff Kubin’s and James Giddens’ testimonies, the need

for the transmission line proposed in this Application was not properly evaluated and was

misevaluated.5 Moreover, facts have changed since the Permian Basin Reliability Plan was

approved warranting re-examining the proposed project.6

       Conversely, in the event the Commission does not deny the Application, the G-9 and G-13

Landowners do not agree with the ALJs’ alternative recommendation that Route 894 be selected.7

The Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA)8 and Commission Rules9 set out criteria the

Commission shall consider in selecting a “best meets” route.                        Yet, the ALJs’ routing

recommendation and evaluation of Route 296 did not include all of the criteria set forth in PURA

and Commission Rules. Instead, the ALJs acknowledged that Route 296 performs favorably on

environmental considerations and noted only one downside: that the centerline of Route 296 as

currently routed runs within 500 feet of Florence Elementary School and two churches. 10 In the

 ALJs’ routing recommendation, the ALJs compared two Central Corridor routes, Routes 487

and 894, based on multiple criteria such as habitable structures, paralleling existing compatible

rights of way, crossing rangeland pasture, and crossing riparian areas. 11 The ALJs, however, did

not include all Focus Routes12 in their routing recommendation analysis, and thus did not recognize

that Route 296 performed similarly, if not better, than Routes 487 and 894 based on the criteria

the ALJs analyzed. As discussed in detail below, should the Commission approve the Application,

the Commission should reject the ALJs’ recommendation and instead select Route 296.

                             II.     PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES 1-4

A. Application Adequacy (Issue 1)

        As noted in the PFD, the Commission has already made a determination on this issue by

denying the appeals of certain intervenors appealing the ALJs’ denial of the route adequacy

challenges.13 Therefore, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners will not address this issue.

B. Notice (Issues 2-3)

        The G-9 and G-13 Landowners agree with the ALJs’ analysis and determination that the

Applicants did not comply with 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 22.52(a)(3) and (a)(4),14 and therefore, do

not have exceptions to this finding. However, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners reserve the right, if

necessary, to respond in replies to exceptions.

 C. Public Input (Issue 4)

       The G-9 and G-13 Landowners do not have issue with the ALJs’ summary of the public

input received by Applicants during the public participation meetings and therefore do not have

exceptions to this issue.15

                 III.       ISSUE RAISED BY THE PARTIES: DUE PROCESS

       The G-9 and G-13 Landowners appreciate the ALJs’ summary of the various issues and

concerns raised due to the compressed procedural schedule and notice problems.16 The G-9 and

G-13 Landowners do not have exceptions to this summary.

                                        IV.   NEED (ISSUES 5-7)

       The G-9 and G-13 Landowners agree with the ALJs’ analysis and recommendation to deny

the Applications because the Applicants did not prove the transmission line projects are necessary

for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.17 However, the G-9 and G-

13 Landowners reserve the right if necessary to respond in replies to exceptions.

                             V.     ROUTING CRITERIA (ISSUES 8-10)

       The ALJs recommend that if the Commission approves the Application, the Commission

should select Route 894 for the 765-kV transmission line for the Bell County East-to-Big Hill

portion of Import Path 2.18 In making this recommendation, the ALJs found Routes 296 and 392

perform favorably on environmental considerations, but found the routes to “have considerable

       16

 downsides.”19 Yet the ALJs noted only one downside for Route 296.20 Disqualifying Route 296,

a route of over 200 miles, because of three structures is unreasonable and unnecessary.

Furthermore, the ALJs failed to evaluate Route 296 using the criteria set forth in PURA and

Commission Rules. The ALJs improperly dismissed Route 296 based on a single “downside” that,

as discussed below, can be mitigated. In considering the best route to select, the ALJs should have

considered Route 296 in relation to Routes 487 and 894 using all applicable criteria. If the ALJs

had done so, then it would have been clear that Route 296 is a superior option.

A. Community Values

        The ALJs properly acknowledge the Commission’s definition of “community values” as

“a shared appreciation of an area or other mutual resource by a national, regional, or local

community.”21 In evaluating the impact of the Focus Routes on community values, the ALJs

discuss (1) the Florence Elementary School, (2) the impact to landowners, and (3) future

development.22

        The PFD includes the impacts of the transmission line, specifically Links F6 and F34

(located on Route 296), noting that the Applicants did not consult with the Texas Education

Agency or the Department of Health and Human Services regarding the potential effects of the

line on the health and safety of the elementary school students. Intervenor Wulff Bluff Creek

Ranch, Ltd.’s witness, Dr. Mark Turnbough, testified that “a utility may make a minor adjustment

mitigate the impact by moving the proposed transmission line closer to Tract 2361.24 Tract 2361

in the proceeding.25 Given this fact, the proximity to the school should not disqualify Route 296.

The G-9 and G-13 Landowners urge the Commission to continue to consider Route 296 in their

analysis of the Focus Routes and ultimately select Route 296. The G-9 and G-13 Landowners

further recommend the Commission’s Order require the Applicants to work with Florence

Elementary School, Texas Education Agency, and the Department of Health and Human Services

and use its best efforts to mitigate any potential health and safety concerns.

        The ALJs additionally describe the Focus Routes’ impact to landowners.26 However, the

ALJs failed to describe important facts. For example, the PFD includes a statement that Route 894

crosses 162.8 miles of rangeland pastures but fails to state that Route 296 crosses less miles of

rangeland pastures, 161.47.27 The ALJs discuss concerns expressed by intervenors but fails to

mention any of the concerns expressed by the G-9 and G-13 Landowners, Bob Guthrie, James

Giddens, and Jeff Kubin. Bob Guthrie owns Tracts 2127 and 2128 and would be directly impacted

by the selection of any of the Focus Routes aside from Route 296.28 Mr. Guthrie’s tracts are made

up of 272 contiguous acres full of live oaks and green pastures known as the Guthrie Ranch.29 The

 Guthrie Ranch is not only a working ranch with three habitable structures, but is a gathering place

for the Guthrie family and a place for the Guthrie grandchildren to build their future homes.30

Link G13 would bisect the Guthrie Ranch in such a way that the Guthries would not be able to

move across their property from the northern portion to the southern portion without crossing

under the transmission line. The transmission line right-of-way would take away much of the

improved grass that his 40 cattle, 200 sheep, and 65 goats use to graze. More critically, the

proposed transmission line would be just over 500 feet from two of the habitable structures on the

property and just over 600 feet from the third habitable structure on the property.31 Even though

one home is just beyond 600 feet from the transmission line, the inhabitants would be just as

impacted as homes within 520 feet. Despite this equal impact, this habitable structure was not

taken into consideration in the total habitable structure count for Link G13.32 Similarly, James

Giddens owns Tracts 2147 and 5142 with eight habitable structures that will be impacted by the

Focus Routes that use Link G13 because Link G13 runs parallel to the property line and will be

visible from those habitable structures, diminishing the enjoyment of the property.33

13.34 The Kubin property consists of one habitable structure located on the 600 acres with a mile

of the McDaniel Branch Creek running through it.35 The Kubin property is a working ranch.36

Not only will the proposed transmission lines destroy the view of the Texas Hill County, it will

B. Recreational and Park Areas

       The PFD’s primary focus with respect to recreational and park areas is the impact of the

proposed transmission line on Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.38

Specifically, the PFD includes two tables showing the number of parks or recreational areas within

1,000 feet of the route centerline, estimated length of ROW within foreground visual zone of

park/recreational areas (miles), and distance from Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge

State Park to Focus Routes.39 The PFD further notes that a viewshed analysis from Texas State

Parks indicated that “a 150- to 200-foot-tall transmission line and tower within 5 miles of a scenic

viewpoint valued for its natural qualities, is likely to be distracting to most visitors.”40 Thus, the

further away the transmission line is from a park, the better.

       With this understanding, the PFD properly discusses the proximity of Link J11 and J22,

located on Route 487 and 894, respectively, to Colorado Bend State Park and the impact of those

Links on the park.41 However, the PFD does not include the J31/J32 Node located on Route 296

in its discussion on the impact to the Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.

C. Aesthetic and Historic Values

         The G-9 and G-13 Landowners do not except to any of the information included in the

ALJs’ description of the aesthetic and historic values subsection of the PFD. The ALJs’ table from

the Environmental Assessment (EA) accurately shows that Route 296 performs similarly to the

other Focus Routes. Specifically, Route 296 crosses the same amount of U.S. or State Highways

as Route 392, and only two more than Routes 487 and 894.43 Route 296 crosses over only two

more recorded cultural resource sites than Routes 894 and 487, and 12 fewer than Route 392.44

Only 18 recorded cultural resource sites are within 1,000 feet of Route 296’s centerline.45 This is

the same amount as Route 487, and only 6 more than Route 894.46 Fifty-three miles of Route 296

cross areas of high archeological/historical site potential which is 1.34 miles less than Route 894.47

         The PFD notes multiple archeological and historical sites located on the Focus Routes that

were not included in the application.48 This is largely because “Burnet County was home to

Comanche, Apache, and many other tribes.”49 Consequently, it would be impossible to find a

similarly to the other Focus Routes, this factor should not weigh against the performance of

Route 296.

D. Environmental Integrity

       The G-9 and G-13 Landowners support the ALJs’ finding that Route 296 performs

favorably on environmental considerations and therefore do not have any exceptions to this

finding. 50 However, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners reserve the right if necessary to respond in

the replies to exceptions.

E. Costs

       In recommending a route, the ALJs note that they did not find cost to be a distinguishing

factor in selecting a route due to the tight range of costs of each route. 51 Despite the ALJs not

taking costs into consideration, the PFD states “[a]pplicants’ best-meets route, Route 894,

performs favorably on cost”52 and notes that Route 296’s cost is $1.685 billion, or 1.20% more

than Route 894.53 The G-9 and G-13 Landowners would like to further highlight the ALJs’

acknowledgment of the contingency of 10 to 15% that is included in the cost estimates. 54 This

means that although one route may be a small percentage more expensive than another, once the

transmission line is built, that route could be less expensive than the originally estimated cost

versus the other route that was initially estimated to be less expensive. This furthers the ALJs’

 position in its route recommendation that cost should not be a determinative factor when the

difference between two lines is 1.20%.

F. Engineering Constraints

        The ALJs mention intervenor Kevin Kennedy’s assertion regarding the Applicants’ failure

to consider Williamson County’s proposed five-level interchange located on Link F34 (on

Route 296).55 This should not be taken into consideration as a disadvantage of Route 296. As the

PFD earlier states, “[t]he Commission has not afforded proposed future development in the same

consideration as existing constraints.”56 The PFD further notes that “[i]nstead, the question is

whether future development that could be affected a proposed route has been initiated in some

readily observable or measurable way on that route.”57 Here, the PFD does not note any readily

observable or measurable initiation of the proposed interchange. Therefore, this development,

under Commission precedent, should not carry the same weight as other existing constraints when

selecting a route.

G. Route Length and Use of Existing Compatible ROWs/Property Lines

        The PFD correctly asserts that the criterion the Commission must use to analyze whether

a route parallels property lines is not “apparent” property lines.58 The PFD also asserts that

“apparent property boundaries” were used in the current application.59 However, the PFD did not

tax-parcel lines but instead refers to the property boundaries of a landowner’s contiguous area of

bisected. Here, Link G13 (on Routes 392, 487, and 894) bisects Tracts 2102, 2103, 2107, 2109,

2128, and 2124.61 With regard to route length, 66% of Link G13 does not parallel apparent

property boundaries.62 This is a severe deviation from PURA and the Commission’s Rules that

could be remedied by selecting Route 296. Further, as the table provided in the PFD shows,

Route 296 parallels apparent property boundaries the furthest and parallels compatible rights-of-

way for 105.3 miles which is significantly longer than Route 894’s 98 miles.

H. Prudent Avoidance

        The ALJs includes Commission Staff’s assertion that Route 487 does not utilize several

links that received significant opposition.63 However, the ALJs fail to include a key piece of

information in Staff’s recommendation of Route 487 based, partially, on this factor. Commission

Staff Witness John Poole had only read a portion of intervenors filed testimonies. Specifically,

Mr. Poole admitted that in his review he alphabetized intervenor direct testimony by first name

and only got through the letter “F” before he submitted his testimony.64 This means Staff’s

        Further, the PFD includes a table from the Environmental Assessment with a breakdown

of the habitable structures located on each of the Focus Routes.65 What the table does not show,

nor does the PFD mention, is the proximity of these habitable structures to the transmission line.

As asserted by the G-9 and G-13 Landowners previously, Link G13 (on Routes 392, 497, and 894)

goes directly against the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance due to the location of pro-se

intervenor Aaron Games’ family home. The Games’ family home is located a mere 175 feet from

the centerline of Link G13.66 This close proximity immensely diminishes the value of the property

financially and the enjoyment of the property as well as creating a nuisance that will ensue for the

Games family who inhabit their home daily as construction and maintenance on the transmission

line will be a continuous occurrence.67 A house located just 75 feet from the right-of-way

unnecessarily exposes a family to the immediate proximity of this 765-kV transmission line. This

should be avoided by selecting another route that does not use Link G13, such as Route 296.

I. Moderation of Impact to Landowners

        In the PFD, the ALJs note that they considered the other routing factors in deciding how to

moderate the impact to the community and landowners.68 While the G-9 and G-13 Landowners

understand how consideration of the other factors can moderate the impact to landowners, the G-

9 and G-13 Landowners recommend the Commission adopt an order that directs Oncor to work

This is in accordance with the modifications made in recent 765-kV transmission applications by

J. Routing Recommendation

        As discussed above, in making a routing recommendation, the ALJs identified only one

“downside” with Route 296.70 In doing so, the ALJs compared Routes 487 and 894 using the other

factors from PURA and Commission Rules.71 It was improper for the ALJs to dismiss Route 296

based on one stated “downside” when PURA and Commission Rules requires a determination on

selection of a route to be based on multiple factors. Had the ALJs considered Route 296 in their

evaluation of the remaining factors, as they did with Routes 487 and 894, then the ALJs would

have seen that Route 296 is the superior route. The ALJs do properly note that Route 296 performs

favorably on environmental considerations due to it utilizing a Colorado River crossing with a pre-

existing infrastructure corridor.72 However, Route 296 also crosses fewer riparian areas than

Routes 894 or 487 and crosses no upland woodlands.73 In addition to performing favorably on

environmental considerations, Route 296 also follows more compatible rights-of-way than

                                  VI.    CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners respectfully request the

Commission modify and adopt a PFD consistent with these Exceptions. The G-9 and G-13

Landowners also request any such other relief to which they have shown themselves entitled.

F. Engineering Constraints

         The ALJs mention intervenor Kevin Kennedy' s assertion regarding the Applicants' failure

to consider Williamson County' s proposed five-level interchange located on Link F34 (on

Route 296).55 This should not be taken into consideration as a disadvantage of Route 296. As the

PFD earlier states, "[t]he Commission has not afforded proposed future development in the same

consideration as existing constraints."56 The PFD further notes that "[ilnstead, the question is

whether future development that could be affected a proposed route has been initiated in some

readily observable or measurable way on that route."57 Here, the PFD does not note any readily

observable or measurable initiation of the proposed interchange. Therefore, this development,

under Commission precedent, should not carry the same weight as other existing constraints when

selecting a route.
